findings.title: forEach callback made async but errors no longer caught by surrounding try/catch
findings.body: The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(...)` was converted to an `async` function so that `getCalendar` can be awaited. However, `Array.prototype.forEach` never awaits the promises returned by its callback and does not propagate rejections to the caller. Previously the callback was synchronous, so any exception thrown inside it (e.g. from `getCalendar`) was thrown synchronously and caught by the surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { ... }` block. Now that the callback is async, any error (including a *synchronous* throw now wrapped into a rejected promise) becomes an unhandled promise rejection that bypasses the try/catch entirely. This both silently swallows/escapes expected error handling and means `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`/`deleteMeeting(...)` are fire-and-forget — the function can return before calendar/video cleanup actually completes.

findings.title: forEach callback made async but errors no longer caught by surrounding try/catch
findings.body: Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: the `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` callback is now async but forEach does not await it or propagate its rejections. The enclosing `try/catch` can no longer catch errors raised inside the callback (including from the now-async `getCalendar` call), and the calendar/video deletion promises are not awaited, so cleanup may not complete before the function proceeds and errors are silently turned into unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged.

findings.title: Async forEach callback not awaited, deletion races with subsequent email send
findings.body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` so the newly-async `getCalendar` call can be awaited inside it, but `forEach` does not wait for the returned promises. As a result the calendar/video deletion work (`calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`, `deleteMeeting(...)`) is fire-and-forget: the code immediately proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and webhook dispatch without waiting for cleanup to finish, and any rejection from this async callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no error handling (there is no try/catch around this block), unlike the pattern used elsewhere in the codebase.

findings.title: Dynamic app imports resolved sequentially instead of in parallel
findings.body: `getVideoAdapters` was rewritten from a synchronous `reduce` into a `for...of` loop that does `await appStore[appName...]` for each credential one at a time. Since `appStore[appName]` is now a dynamic import `Promise`, awaiting them sequentially in a loop serializes the resolution of all needed app modules instead of resolving them concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`). For bookings with multiple video credentials this adds unnecessary latency compared to resolving all needed app chunks in parallel.

findings.title: getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise-valued 'calendar' field without updating its own signature
findings.body: `getCalendar` was changed to return `Promise<Calendar | null>`, but `getCalendarCredentials` (still a synchronous function) stores this directly as `calendar` in the objects it returns: `{ integration: app, credential, calendar }`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`. `getCalendarCredentials` is exported from this module and may be consumed elsewhere in the codebase (not part of this diff) expecting a resolved `Calendar | null` value as before; such call sites would now silently receive an unresolved Promise instead of a calendar instance, a breaking change that isn't reflected in the function's own type signature (still implicitly synchronous).

findings.title: All app-store dynamic imports are started eagerly on module load, not on demand
findings.body: The appStore object stores the results of calling `import("./x")` directly as object values, e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`. Because `import()` is invoked immediately when the object literal is evaluated, every one of the 29 app packages begins loading as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is first imported anywhere (e.g. from `CalendarManager`, `EventManager`, `videoClient`, or any tRPC router), regardless of whether a given request only needs a single app. This does not provide true lazy/on-demand loading per app; it only defers resolution behind a Promise while still eagerly kicking off every import at module-initialization time, which may add unnecessary module loading overhead especially in short-lived serverless/edge invocations.

findings.title: No test coverage added for the sync-to-async conversion of core calendar/video/payment functions
findings.body: This PR changes the public async contract of many widely used, previously-synchronous functions (`getCalendar`, `CalendarManager.deleteEvent/createEvent/updateEvent`, `videoClient.getVideoAdapters/deleteMeeting/createMeeting/updateMeeting`, `handlePayment`/`deletePayment`'s appStore lookup, etc.) across the booking cancellation, rescheduling, and payment refund flows. No new or updated unit/integration tests are included to verify that callers correctly await these functions and that behavior (ordering of calendar deletion vs. email/webhook sending, error propagation) is preserved after the conversion, despite several call sites exhibiting the forEach/async anti-pattern that silently changes error-handling and ordering semantics.
